stories.headline: Democrats sweep US midterms; Trump accepts losses as Republicans blame Iran war
stories.summary: Democrats won control of both chambers of the US Congress in the November 2026 midterm elections, flipping the Senate and the House and adding governor and state-level gains, including full Democratic control of Pennsylvania's state government from 2027. All 435 House seats and 35 of the 100 Senate seats were contested; going into the vote Republicans held the House 220–215 and the Senate 53–47 after the 2024 elections, with Vice-President JD Vance's tie-breaking vote in the Senate. President Donald Trump publicly accepted the losses, while Vice-President Vance and other Republicans attributed the defeat to voter anger over the Iran war, inflation, the 'America First' agenda and Washington's relationship with Israel; Trump defended the campaign against Tehran as necessary to stop Iran acquiring nuclear weapons. The Republican House Speaker said he would step down, and Ukraine's President voiced hope that Democratic gains would bring more US help for Ukraine. Analysts expect the new congressional majorities to constrain the White House on foreign policy while Democratic-run states advance domestic legislation on election reform, marijuana legalisation and minimum wages.
stories.whyItMatters: A divided US government resets the balance between the White House and Congress, with direct consequences for the Iran conflict, Ukraine aid, sanctions and alliance management — all inputs into India's strategic autonomy and multi-alignment calculus.

stories.headline: US sanctions Indian, Turkish firms over Iran oil shadow fleet
stories.summary: Washington has imposed sanctions on India-based individuals and companies — including a couple — along with a Turkish firm, accusing them of helping Iran move petroleum in defiance of international restrictions. The Indian entities are alleged to have supplied false maritime identities, vessel registrations and certifications to tankers carrying Iranian crude, enabling Tehran's 'shadow fleet' to disguise its cargoes. The Turkish firm was targeted separately over support for Iran's airlines. The designations form part of the Trump administration's 'Operation Economic Outcast', which seeks to choke off the oil revenue funding Iran's war with the United States and Israel. The action extends the reach of US secondary sanctions to Indian private actors, raising fresh compliance and energy-security questions for Indian shipping, trading and refining firms.

static.topic: US Secondary Sanctions and Iran's 'Shadow Fleet'
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Effect of policies and politics of developed countries on India's interests; economic sanctions
static.whatIsIt: Secondary sanctions are US penalties imposed on non-US persons and entities — not merely on the target state — for facilitating trade with a sanctioned country such as Iran. They are administered mainly by the US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) through the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) list, which freezes assets and bars US persons from dealing with listed parties. Iran's 'shadow fleet' refers to ageing tankers with opaque ownership, falsified or repeatedly switched flags, disabled AIS transponders and ship-to-ship transfers used to move oil outside Western insurance and tracking systems.
static.background: US sanctions on Iran date back to the 1979 hostage crisis and were broadened through the 1996 Iran-Libya Sanctions Act and successive executive orders. The 2015 JCPOA lifted nuclear-related sanctions; the US withdrew in May 2018 and reimposed 'maximum pressure' sanctions, ending crude import waivers for countries including India in May 2019. CAATSA (2017) added a legal framework for sanctioning third-country actors. Enforcement against shadow-fleet facilitators has intensified since 2023.
static.geography: Enforced globally through the US financial system; the shadow fleet operates mainly in the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz, the Malacca Strait and anchorage areas such as Fujairah and off Malaysia.
static.socioEconomic: India's refiners stopped Iranian crude imports in 2019, but Indian shipping, ship-management, insurance and trading firms remain exposed to designation risk, which raises compliance costs and can cut access to dollar financing.
static.whyInNews: The US designated India-based individuals and companies, including a couple, and a Turkish firm for providing false maritime identities and certifications to vessels transporting Iranian petroleum.
static.wayForward: Indian firms need robust sanctions-compliance and vessel due-diligence systems; India can pursue rupee-based settlement, diversify crude sourcing and press for clarity on waivers for strategic projects such as Chabahar.
prelimsPointers: OFAC, under the US Treasury, administers most US sanctions and maintains the SDN list.
CAATSA (2017) allows the US to sanction entities dealing with Iran, Russia and North Korea.
AIS (Automatic Identification System) is a maritime tracking system frequently switched off by shadow-fleet tankers.
India halted Iranian crude imports in 2019 after the US ended its sanctions waiver.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how the extraterritorial reach of US secondary sanctions constrains India's strategic autonomy and energy security, and suggest a policy response.

static.topic: India–Iran Relations and the Chabahar Project
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and its neighbourhood; bilateral relations with Iran; connectivity
static.whatIsIt: India–Iran ties rest on energy, connectivity and cultural links. Chabahar port, on Iran's Makran coast in Sistan-Baluchestan province, is India's key connectivity project, giving access to Afghanistan and Central Asia while bypassing Pakistan. India Ports Global Ltd (IPGL) operates the Shahid Beheshti terminal.
static.background: India, Iran and Afghanistan signed the Chabahar trilateral agreement in May 2016. India supplied cranes and equipment and handled wheat and pulse shipments to Afghanistan through the port. In May 2024, IPGL signed a 10-year contract with Iran's Ports and Maritime Organisation to operate the terminal. Chabahar is also a node of the International North–South Transport Corridor (INSTC), an India–Iran–Russia initiative agreed in 2000. US sanctions have repeatedly complicated financing and equipment supply.
static.geography: Chabahar lies on the Gulf of Oman, outside the Strait of Hormuz, giving it strategic value as an alternative to Pakistan's China-operated Gwadar port to its east.
static.socioEconomic: The port supports Indian trade with Afghanistan and Central Asia, regional humanitarian shipments, and development of Iran's relatively underdeveloped Sistan-Baluchestan region.
static.whyInNews: The fresh US designations on Indian entities over Iranian oil come amid continuing uncertainty over sanctions waivers affecting Chabahar and India–Iran trade.
static.wayForward: India should keep Chabahar and the INSTC operational through sustained diplomatic engagement on waivers, expand rupee-based trade mechanisms, and balance its US partnership against its Iran connectivity interests.
prelimsPointers: Chabahar is Iran's only oceanic port, located on the Gulf of Oman.
India, Iran and Afghanistan signed the Chabahar agreement in May 2016.
The INSTC, agreed in 2000, links India to Russia via Iran and Central Asia.
Pakistan's Gwadar port, developed by China, lies east of Chabahar.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the strategic significance of Chabahar for India's connectivity to Central Asia and the constraints imposed by US sanctions.

static.topic: The Iran Nuclear Issue and the JCPOA
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global groupings and agreements affecting India's interests; nuclear non-proliferation
static.whatIsIt: The Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) is the 2015 agreement between Iran and the P5+1 (US, UK, France, Russia, China, Germany) plus the EU, under which Iran accepted limits on its nuclear programme in return for relief from nuclear-related sanctions. It was endorsed by UN Security Council Resolution 2231.
static.background: Signed in July 2015 after years of negotiation. The US withdrew in May 2018 and reimposed sanctions. Iran progressively reduced compliance from 2019 and enriched uranium to higher levels. The JCPOA contains a 'snapback' provision allowing participants to restore UN sanctions; the E3 (UK, France, Germany) triggered this mechanism in 2025, reviving UN sanctions on Iran. Talks to revive the deal have remained stalled.
static.geography: Iran's nuclear facilities include Natanz, Fordow and Isfahan; the Strait of Hormuz carries a large share of global seaborne oil trade.
static.socioEconomic: Sanctions have squeezed Iran's oil exports and currency, while oil-importing economies such as India face price and supply volatility whenever West Asia tensions escalate.
static.whyInNews: The US crackdown on Iran's oil exports — including sanctions on Indian and Turkish entities — is part of the wider pressure campaign linked to Iran's nuclear programme and its conflict with the US and Israel.
static.wayForward: A durable diplomatic settlement on Iran's nuclear programme is needed to stabilise oil markets; India should maintain channels with all parties and hedge its energy supplies.

UNSC Resolution 2231 (2015) endorsed the JCPOA.

stories.headline: US midterms: a divided Congress and India's room to manoeuvre
stories.summary: The 2026 US midterm results have delivered major losses to President Donald Trump's Republican Party, reshaping the political arithmetic in Washington. Indian commentary suggests the outcome matters less for the substance of India–US ties than for the space India has to manoeuvre in geopolitics, particularly on the Iran war, purchases of Russian oil, a pending trade deal, immigration and China policy. Vice-President JD Vance publicly attributed the Republican setback to the Iran war, while US coverage also points to cost-of-living and working-class discontent as drivers. Indian analysts argue that Delhi must look beyond the federal executive and engage the 'many Americas' — Congress, states, business and society. The net effect is a more contested, less predictable US policy environment in which India's strategic autonomy will be tested.
stories.whyItMatters: US domestic political cycles directly shape the external environment in which India pursues strategic autonomy — sanctions, energy sourcing, trade and technology access all move with Washington's politics. This is a live GS-II case study on how the policies and politics of a developed country affect India's interests.

stories.headline: India draws $400 billion in preliminary renewable investment pledges
stories.summary: The government has said India attracted roughly $400 billion in preliminary investment pledges in the renewable energy sector, announced at the Bharat Renewable Energy Summit. The commitments are indicative rather than contracted, and the government intends to review the proposals before they translate into projects. Alongside the pledges, official attention is on advancing grid-scale storage and on meeting India's targets for expanding non-fossil energy capacity. The development signals strong investor interest in India's clean-energy pipeline, but the gap between pledges and commissioned capacity will depend on power purchase agreements, transmission readiness, land and domestic manufacturing. Storage is being positioned as the critical enabler for absorbing a larger share of variable renewables.
stories.whyItMatters: Renewable investment and grid-scale storage sit at the intersection of India's energy security, climate commitments and infrastructure financing — a recurring GS-III theme. The pledge-versus-commissioning gap is a useful case study for evaluating the credibility of investment announcements.

perspectives.take: A business-paper framing that foregrounds the headline investment figure while flagging that the pledges are preliminary and will be reviewed, and links them to grid-scale storage and non-fossil capacity goals.

static.background: India's renewable push began with a dedicated non-conventional energy department in the early 1980s, later upgraded into the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy. The Jawaharlal Nehru National Solar Mission (2010) set early solar targets under the National Action Plan on Climate Change. Targets were progressively raised — from 175 GW of renewables by 2022 to 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030 — and the 2021 Panchamrit pledges added net zero by 2070.

static.background: As the share of variable renewables rises, storage becomes essential for grid stability. stories.headline: Midterms may reshape US policy on China, Taiwan and tariffs
stories.summary: Democratic victories in the US midterm elections have given the party control of both chambers of Congress, according to reports, potentially constraining President Donald Trump's foreign-policy room. The outcome is being watched for its effect on Washington's approach to China, Taiwan arms sales and tariff policy, though business executives caution that near-term cost relief for firms is unlikely. Taiwan's defence minister said cross-party US support for Taipei's defence capabilities is expected to continue in Congress. Canada sees renewed pressure on the White House to reach a trade deal as Canada-US talks resume. The results are also being interpreted as a rebuke of the US-Israel relationship, while think-tank analysis highlights broader foreign-policy consequences.

stories.headline: Centre proposes immediate suspension of drug licences for quality failures
stories.summary: The Centre has proposed amending India's drug rules so that manufacturing licences can be suspended immediately when quality failures are detected, instead of allowing substandard medicines to stay in circulation while manufacturers rectify defects. Alongside this, the draft changes tighten microbial contamination norms under Schedule M, which prescribes Good Manufacturing Practices for pharmaceutical units. The proposals, reported across national business and general dailies, mark a shift from a warning-and-rectify approach towards risk-based, precautionary regulatory action. They follow persistent concerns over contamination, failed batch tests and export rejections that have dented confidence in Indian-made medicines. The amendments are at the draft stage, with stakeholder comments being sought before final notification.
stories.whyItMatters: Directly relevant to GS-II health governance and regulatory capacity, and to GS-III debates on India's pharmaceutical industry and export reputation as the 'pharmacy of the world'. It also illustrates how subordinate legislation under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act is used to deliver public-health outcomes.

perspectives.take: Frames the move primarily as a consumer-safety crackdown, foregrounding the power to suspend licences at once rather than after prolonged proceedings.
Business-and-policy lens: highlights the stricter microbial contamination norms under Schedule M and the compliance burden this places on manufacturers.
Policy-economy framing: stresses the intent to stop substandard medicines from remaining in the market while firms address quality failures and regulatory concerns.

static.topic: Drug Regulation in India: CDSCO and the Drugs and Cosmetics Act
static.syllabusNode: Social Justice — Health Governance and Regulatory Institutions
static.whatIsIt: India's drug regulatory framework rests on the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945, which govern manufacture, sale, import and quality standards of drugs and cosmetics. The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO), under the Directorate General of Health Services in the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, is the national regulator, while state drug controllers license and inspect most manufacturing and sale units.
static.background: The 1940 Act followed recommendations of the Drugs Enquiry Committee (Chopra Committee) of 1930, which flagged the need for uniform drug quality control. The Rules of 1945 operationalised it, with Schedule M laying down Good Manufacturing Practices. Advisory bodies include the Drugs Technical Advisory Board (DTAB) and the Drugs Consultative Committee. The New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019 updated approval pathways, and recent amendments introduced risk-based inspections and central approval requirements for certain categories of drugs.
static.socioEconomic: India is among the world's largest suppliers of generic medicines and vaccines by volume, so domestic quality failures carry both public-health and export-reputation consequences, particularly for small and mid-sized manufacturers.
static.whyInNews: The Centre has proposed allowing immediate suspension of manufacturing licences when quality failures are detected, rather than permitting substandard medicines to remain in circulation during rectification.
static.wayForward: Strengthen inspectorates and accredited testing laboratories, institutionalise risk-based and unannounced inspections, expand track-and-trace of batches, publish test results transparently, and calibrate penalties to the severity of harm.
prelimsPointers: CDSCO functions under the Directorate General of Health Services, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.
Drug regulation is a shared responsibility: the Centre handles approvals, standards and imports, while states license and inspect most manufacturing and retail units.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how regulatory federalism and capacity gaps between central and state drug authorities shape the effectiveness of drug quality enforcement in India.

static.topic: Schedule M and Good Manufacturing Practices
static.syllabusNode: Science and Technology — Health, Pharmaceuticals and Biotechnology
static.whatIsIt: Schedule M of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 specifies Good Manufacturing Practices — requirements for premises, plant and equipment, hygiene, personnel, quality control and limits on contamination — that pharmaceutical manufacturers must meet.
static.background: Schedule M has been revised over the decades to align with international norms, with a revised version notified in 2023 and phased compliance timelines for manufacturers of different sizes. WHO Good Manufacturing Practices certification, which depends on Schedule M compliance, is a prerequisite for many export markets and for WHO prequalification of medicines.
static.socioEconomic: Tighter norms raise compliance costs, which weigh most heavily on small and medium manufacturers, but they also protect patients and preserve access to regulated export markets.
static.whyInNews: The Centre has proposed stricter microbial contamination norms under Schedule M as part of the same package of quality reforms.
static.wayForward: Pair stricter norms with credible testing infrastructure, technical handholding and phased timelines for MSME units, so that compliance is achievable rather than merely punitive.
prelimsPointers: Schedule M forms part of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 and prescribes Good Manufacturing Practices.
WHO GMP certification is a prerequisite for WHO prequalification and for entry into several regulated export markets.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss whether tightening manufacturing standards can simultaneously improve patient safety and the competitiveness of India's pharmaceutical sector.

static.topic: Delegated Legislation and Rule-Making in India
static.whatIsIt: Much of India's regulatory detail is set through subordinate legislation — rules, regulations and notifications framed by the executive under authority delegated by a parent Act. The Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 are subordinate legislation under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, and draft amendments are published for objections before final notification.
static.background: Parliament enacts the parent statute, which becomes law after passage by both Houses and Presidential assent under Article 111. Rules framed under it are typically required to be laid before Parliament, and the Committee on Subordinate Legislation scrutinises them for conformity with the parent Act. Ordinances under Article 123 are a separate, temporary route available when Parliament is not in session.
static.whyInNews: The proposed suspension powers and contamination norms are being brought in through draft amendments to the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules rather than fresh primary legislation.
static.wayForward: Ensure meaningful consultation periods, publish stakeholder comments and rationale, and strengthen parliamentary scrutiny of subordinate legislation so that executive rule-making remains accountable.
prelimsPointers: Subordinate legislation is framed by the executive under authority delegated by a parent Act and is generally laid before Parliament.
Parliamentary Committees on Subordinate Legislation examine rules and regulations for conformity with the parent statute.
static.mainsAngle: Assess whether India's practice of regulating sensitive sectors such as pharmaceuticals through delegated legislation adequately balances flexibility with democratic accountability.

stories.headline: Delhi SIR: SC leaves 'logical discrepancy' legality open; ECI defends Form 6 use
stories.summary: The Supreme Court, hearing the challenge to the Delhi Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, has said that the legality of the 'logical discrepancy' ground — used to flag or remove electors — remains undecided. The Election Commission has defended its practice of using Form 6, the application for inclusion of a name, in respect of electors deleted during the exercise. Reporting on the proceedings indicates that the Commission's justification did not directly address the specific questions the Court had posed. The matter therefore continues, with the substantive question of what grounds may lawfully justify deletion still open.
stories.whyItMatters: It tests the constitutional limits of the ECI's Article 324 powers over roll revision against the right to vote under Article 326 — a recurring GS-II theme linking constitutional bodies, judicial review and electoral integrity.

static.topic: Supreme Court, High Courts & Judicial Review
static.whatIsIt: The Supreme Court (Art. 124) is the apex court and guardian of the Constitution; High Courts (Art. 214) sit at the state level. Judicial review is the power of courts to test legislative and executive action against the Constitution.
static.background: The collegium system evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998). Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic-structure doctrine. PILs expanded access to justice from the late 1970s. Articles 32 (SC) and 226 (HC) provide writ jurisdiction.
static.whyInNews: In the Delhi SIR litigation, the Supreme Court observed that the legality of the 'logical discrepancy' ground used to flag or delete electors remains undecided, keeping the substantive question open even as proceedings continue.
static.wayForward: The Court should record reasoned findings on each challenged ground rather than leaving core legality questions open, so that the ECI's roll-revision framework acquires clear constitutional boundaries.

static.topic: Election Commission of India & Electoral Roll Revision (SIR)
static.whatIsIt: The ECI is a constitutional body under Article 324 with superintendence, direction and control of elections. Electoral rolls are prepared and revised under the Representation of the People Act, 1950, with Form 6 for inclusion of a name, Form 7 for objections/deletion and Form 8 for corrections.
static.background: Roll revision is a routine annual/quarterly exercise; 'Special Intensive Revision' (SIR) is a house-to-house verification variant used when the ECI decides a roll needs intensive scrutiny. An SIR was conducted in Bihar in 2025, and a similar exercise was taken up for Delhi, drawing litigation over deletions, notice and hearing, and the grounds used to flag electors.
static.geography: Delhi (NCT) and Bihar are the principal theatres of the current SIR litigation.
static.socioEconomic: Deletions can affect access to welfare and documentation often linked to electoral-roll presence; the burden of re-registration falls disproportionately on migrants, the poor and first-time voters.
static.whyInNews: The ECI defended its use of Form 6 for voters deleted during SIR; The Wire reported that this defence does not answer the Supreme Court's specific questions, while the Court said the legality of 'logical discrepancy' remains undecided.
static.wayForward: Codify clear, published criteria and a reasoned, appealable deletion process with adequate notice and hearing, ensuring the burden of proof does not shift to the elector.

Electoral rolls are prepared under the RP Act, 1950; conduct of elections is governed by the RP Act, 1951.
Form 6 = inclusion of name; Form 7 = objection/deletion; Form 8 = correction.

stories.headline: Seven-judge bench disposes reference on states' power to levy sales tax surcharge
stories.summary: A seven-judge bench of the Supreme Court has disposed of a reference on whether states can impose a surcharge or additional levy on sales tax. The reference had raised questions about the scope of state taxation powers and the constitutional balance between Union and State fiscal authority. Live Law reports that the bench held the reference academic, while Supreme Court Observer describes the outcome as the Court disposing of the long-pending question. The disposal removes the immediate reference but does not by itself resolve every future dispute over state levies. The development is relevant to federalism because it touches on how far states may tax transactions within their legislative domain.
stories.whyItMatters: Tests understanding of fiscal federalism, Seventh Schedule taxation entries, and the Supreme Court's role in resolving constitutional questions between Centre and States.

static.topic: Tropical Cyclones and Indian Monsoon Variability

static.whatIsIt: Tropical cyclones are intense low-pressure systems forming over warm ocean waters, characterised by a calm eye, spiral rain bands and strong winds. In India they develop over the North Indian Ocean — the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea — and the Bay of Bengal, with its warmer waters and favourable wind patterns, is the more cyclone-prone basin.
static.background: The Indian monsoon is a seasonal reversal of winds driven by differential heating, the northward shift of the ITCZ and the Tibetan Plateau's role as a heat pump, delivering roughly 75% of annual rainfall in June–September. Cyclones forming in the pre- and post-monsoon months interact with monsoon circulation and with phenomena such as El Niño/La Niña and the Indian Ocean Dipole, which modulate rainfall and storm behaviour. Peninsular rivers are rain-fed and seasonal, so heavy cyclonic rainfall translates quickly into flooding.
static.geography: The eastern coast — Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha and West Bengal — faces the Bay of Bengal, the most cyclone-active part of the North Indian Ocean. The Western Ghats and the Deccan plateau shape drainage and rain-shadow patterns across the peninsula.
static.socioEconomic: Cyclones damage crops, fishing livelihoods, housing, roads and power infrastructure, and trigger displacement in coastal districts. Inland, the same systems bring urban flooding and, in the north, contrasting conditions such as shallow fog and deteriorating air quality in Delhi NCR.
static.whyInNews: IMD has warned of heavy rainfall and thunderstorms over Tamil Nadu, Odisha and Andhra Pradesh as the remnants of Cyclone Murasu persist, following Cyclone Arnab; shallow fog and a slipping AQI are reported in Delhi NCR.
static.wayForward: Strengthen multi-hazard early warning dissemination down to the panchayat level, integrate cyclone risk into coastal land-use and building codes, and invest in climate-resilient infrastructure so that repeated storms do not repeatedly destroy the same assets.
prelimsPointers: Himalayan rivers are perennial (snow-fed); peninsular rivers are largely rain-fed and seasonal.

stories.headline: NASA's Swift telescope burns up after 22 years; failed robotic rescue sealed its fate
stories.summary: NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, a 3,200-lb space telescope launched in 2004 to hunt gamma-ray bursts, re-entered Earth's atmosphere and burned up in November 2026, ending a 22-year mission. NASA had ended science operations on 20 October 2026, when the observatory was orbiting roughly 275 km above Earth and steadily losing altitude. An earlier attempt to send a robotic spacecraft to boost Swift back to a higher, stable orbit failed, leaving no way to arrest its decay. The episode illustrates how atmospheric drag, ageing hardware and the difficulty of satellite servicing determine the end-of-life of space assets.
stories.whyItMatters: It feeds GS-III Science & Technology questions on space missions, satellite servicing and end-of-life disposal, and links to wider debates on space debris, orbital sustainability and space governance.

static.background: Ramsar Convention (1971) protects wetlands; India has 80+ Ramsar sites. Project Tiger (1973) and Project Elephant (1992) anchor species conservation. The 30x30 target aims to protect 30% of land and sea by 2030.
static.socioEconomic: Balancing conservation with development and community rights (FRA); human-wildlife conflict management.
static.whyInNews: The COP30 deforestation roadmap highlights forest loss, a driver of biodiversity decline, and links climate and biodiversity agendas.
static.wayForward: Integrate forest and biodiversity goals, strengthen community rights, and scale up conservation finance.
prelimsPointers: India's biodiversity hotspots: Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats-Sri Lanka, Sundaland/Nicobar.
World Wetlands Day: 2 February.
static.mainsAngle: Balancing conservation with development and community rights (FRA); human-wildlife conflict management.

prelims: Brazil's COP30 presidency released a deforestation roadmap on 3 November, aiming to guide global action on ending forest loss.
The roadmap has been noted for both its promises and its omissions, including unresolved issues.
Deforestation is a major source of greenhouse gas emissions and biodiversity loss.
Global forest governance links the UNFCCC, Paris Agreement, CBD, and the 30x30 biodiversity target.
stories.mainsQuestion: Discuss the significance of the Brazil-led deforestation roadmap under the COP30 presidency for global climate and biodiversity governance. How can India balance forest conservation with its development imperatives?

onThisDay.title: India launches Mars Orbiter Mission
onThisDay.description: India launched the Mars Orbiter Mission (Mangalyaan), its first interplanetary probe, on 5 November 2013. It made India the first Asian nation to reach Martian orbit and the first country to do so on its maiden attempt.
onThisDay.upscLink: Science & Technology: India's space programme and interplanetary exploration.

onThisDay.title: Suez Crisis: British and French paratroopers land in Egypt
onThisDay.description: During the Suez Crisis, British and French paratroopers landed in Egypt after a week-long bombing campaign. The intervention followed Egypt's nationalisation of the Suez Canal and drew global Cold War tensions.
onThisDay.upscLink: World History: decolonization, Cold War and West Asian geopolitics.

onThisDay.title: France and British Empire declare war on Ottoman Empire
onThisDay.description: In World War I, France and the British Empire declared war on the Ottoman Empire. This widened the conflict into the Middle East and set the stage for the post-war redrawing of boundaries.
onThisDay.upscLink: World History: First World War and redrawal of boundaries.

onThisDay.title: Saddam Hussein sentenced to death
onThisDay.description: Former Iraqi President Saddam Hussein and two co-defendants were sentenced to death in the al-Dujail trial for the 1982 massacre of 148 Shia Muslims. The trial was conducted by the Iraqi High Tribunal after the 2003 US-led invasion.
onThisDay.upscLink: International Relations: international tribunals and West Asian politics.

onThisDay.title: China's Chang'e 1 enters lunar orbit
onThisDay.description: China's first lunar satellite, Chang'e 1, entered orbit around the Moon. It marked a major step in China's space programme and its growing capabilities in lunar exploration.
